reviewNote: Written for GoHard against the sources listed here (ACSM 2009 position stand; Ramos-Campo et al. 2024 meta-analysis). It awaits review by the owner and a qualified coach. General information about exercises and plan structure, not medical advice or a diagnosis.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults
sources.publisher: Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2009 (American College of Sports Medicine)

sources.title: Efficacy of Split Versus Full-Body Resistance Training on Strength and Muscle Growth: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
sources.publisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2024; 38(7):1330–1340 (Ramos-Campo et al.)

splits.name: Full Body
splits.summary: Every session trains the whole body: a squat or hinge, a press, a pull and core work.
splits.organisation: Full body A, B and C use different exercises for the same movement patterns. Two days: A and B. Three days: A, B and C. Other day counts rotate A → B → C.
splits.days: 2–3 days a week, or a rotation over more days
benefits: Each muscle group is trained in every session, so the week stays balanced even if you miss a day.
Two or three sessions are enough to train everything more than once a week.
Every session has the same shape, so it is simple to follow.
limitations: Each session covers every area, so there is less room for extra sets for any one muscle.
Heavy lower-body and upper-body lifts share a session.
Training on back-to-back days works the same muscles again.

splits.name: Upper / Lower
splits.organisation: Upper A, Lower A, Upper B, Lower B. Four days: one each. Two days: Upper A and Lower A. Other day counts rotate the four across weeks.
splits.days: 4 days a week, or a rotation over 2–3
benefits: Each half of the body is trained twice in four sessions.
Each session covers half the body, so it has fewer exercises than a full-body session.
Upper and lower days can follow each other because they work different muscles.
limitations: With three days the four workouts rotate, so a full round takes more than a week.
Lower days with squats and deadlifts are demanding.
Arm and shoulder accessories come at the end of the upper days, after the main presses and pulls.

splits.name: Push / Pull / Legs
splits.summary: Pressing, pulling and legs each get their own day.
splits.organisation: Push (chest, shoulders, triceps), Pull (back, biceps, rear shoulders), Legs. Three days: once each. Six days: all three twice. Other day counts rotate Push → Pull → Legs.
splits.days: 3 or 6 days a week; rotates over other counts
benefits: Each session focuses on muscles that work together, so several exercises fit for them.
A clear rule for what each day trains.
On six days, each area is trained twice a week.
limitations: On three days, each area is trained once a week.
A missed day leaves that area untrained until it comes round again.
Six sessions a week is a large time commitment.

splits.name: Push / Pull, legs included
splits.summary: Two kinds of day: push days carry the knee-dominant leg work, pull days the hip-dominant work.
splits.organisation: Push A, Pull A, Push B, Pull B. Squats, leg press and split squats sit on push days; Romanian deadlifts, deadlifts, hip thrusts and leg curls on pull days.
splits.days: 4 days a week, or 2 (Push A and Pull A)
benefits: Legs are trained on every day, split by movement, instead of one separate leg day.
On four days, each area is trained twice a week.
Upper-body and leg work are spread evenly across the week.
limitations: Every session includes leg work, which some people find tiring on consecutive days.
Sessions are longer than an upper-body-only day.
The A and B days use different exercises, so there is more to learn.

splits.name: Upper / Lower + Push / Pull / Legs
splits.summary: Five sessions: an upper and a lower day, then push, pull and legs.
benefits: Each muscle group is trained about twice across the five sessions.
Combines whole upper and lower days with focused push, pull and leg days.
limitations: Needs five sessions a week; a missed one leaves its areas trained once that week.
Five different workouts to learn.

splits.name: Body-part split
splits.summary: One main area per session: chest, back, legs, shoulders and arms.
benefits: Many sets for one area in a single session.
Each session has one clear focus.
An area trained on one day has the rest of the week before it is trained directly again.
limitations: Each area is trained directly once a week.
A missed session means that area is not trained directly that week.
Needs five sessions a week.

splits.name: Custom
splits.summary: Your own workout names, exercises and order.
splits.organisation: As you build it: name each different workout once, then place them on weekdays or in a rotating cycle.
benefits: Fits any schedule or preference.
You choose every exercise.
limitations: No starting exercises: you add every exercise yourself.
Balancing the muscle groups across the week is up to you.

cues: Bar on the upper back, feet about shoulder-width apart.
Brace your trunk before each rep.
Bend at the hips and knees together, knees following the line of your toes.
Go as deep as you can while your back stays in the same position, then stand up.
benefits: Trains several large leg muscles at once.
Easy to load in small steps.
limitations: Needs a rack, and safety arms or a spotter for heavy sets.
Takes practice to learn.

cues: Feet flat, shoulder blades pulled back and down.
Lower the bar to the middle of your chest under control.
Press up until your arms are straight.
benefits: Trains the main pressing muscles together.
Easy to load in small steps.
limitations: Needs safety arms or a spotter for heavy sets.
Needs a bench and rack.

cues: Hinge forward with a flat back, knees slightly bent.
Pull the bar towards your lower ribs.
Lower it under control without letting your back round.
benefits: Trains the whole upper back with a load that is easy to increase.
limitations: Holding the bent-over position also works the lower back, which can limit the weight.

cues: Bar over the middle of your feet, shins close to it.
Brace, flatten your back, then push the floor away.
Keep the bar close to your legs all the way up.
Lower it by pushing your hips back first.
benefits: Trains most of the back of the body in one lift.
Easy to load in small steps.
limitations: Demanding, so it usually gets the longest rest.
Takes practice to learn.

cues: Stand tall, squeeze your glutes and brace.
Press the bar straight up, moving your head back slightly to let it pass.
Finish with the bar over the middle of your feet.
benefits: Trains the shoulders and triceps while standing.
limitations: Heavy loads are harder to manage than in the bench press.
Needs comfortable overhead shoulder movement.

cues: Sit with your thighs under the pads.
Pull the bar to your upper chest, elbows down and back.
Let it rise under control until your arms are straight.
benefits: The weight can be set below body weight, unlike a pull-up.
limitations: Needs a cable machine.

cues: Start standing, knees slightly bent.
Push your hips back and slide the bar down your thighs with a flat back.
Stop when your hamstrings are stretched, then stand up by driving your hips forward.
benefits: Trains the hamstrings and glutes through a long range.
limitations: Range depends on hamstring flexibility; going lower by rounding the back defeats the purpose.

cues: Feet flat on the platform about shoulder-width apart.
Lower until your knees are well bent without your lower back lifting off the pad.
Press back up without locking your knees hard.
benefits: Trains the legs heavily with little balance or back demand.
limitations: Needs a machine.
Does not train balance or trunk control.

cues: Bench at a low incline.
Lower the dumbbells to the sides of your upper chest.
Press up and slightly in.
benefits: Each arm works on its own, so both sides do equal work.
limitations: Getting heavy dumbbells into position takes practice.

cues: Shoulder blades back, feet flat.
Lower the dumbbells to chest level with elbows at a comfortable angle.
Press up until your arms are straight.
benefits: Each arm works on its own.
No rack or spotter needed to fail safely: the dumbbells can be lowered to the sides.
limitations: Heavy dumbbells are awkward to get into position.

cues: One hand and knee on a bench, back flat.
Pull the dumbbell towards your hip.
Lower it until your arm is straight.
benefits: One side at a time, with the bench supporting your back.
limitations: Each side is done separately, so it takes longer.

cues: Sit tall with a slight bend in your knees.
Pull the handle to your lower ribs, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Let your arms straighten under control.
benefits: Steady resistance with your back supported by sitting upright.
limitations: Needs a cable machine.

cues: Hold one dumbbell upright against your chest.
Sit down between your heels with your chest up.
Stand up by pushing through your whole foot.
benefits: A simple way to learn the squat with one dumbbell.
limitations: The weight you can hold limits how heavy it can get.

cues: Take a long step forward and lower your back knee towards the floor.
Keep your front knee in line with your toes.
Push off the front foot into the next step.
benefits: Trains one leg at a time and challenges balance.
limitations: Needs space to walk.
Balance limits the load.

cues: Set the pad just above your heels.
Curl the pad towards you.
Return slowly until your legs are almost straight.
benefits: Trains the hamstrings by bending the knee, which hip-hinge lifts such as the Romanian deadlift do little of.
limitations: Needs a machine.

cues: Seated or standing, dumbbells at shoulder height.
Press up until your arms are straight.
Lower under control back to shoulder height.
benefits: Each arm works on its own.
Seated, the back support makes it steadier.
limitations: Needs comfortable overhead shoulder movement.

cues: Slight bend in your elbows.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides to about shoulder height.
Lower slowly.
benefits: Targets the side of the shoulder, which presses work less.
limitations: Only light weights are practical.

cues: Elbows by your sides.
Curl the dumbbells up without swinging your body.
Lower until your arms are straight.
benefits: Direct work for the biceps.
limitations: Trains a small muscle group only.

cues: Elbows tucked at your sides.
Push the handle down until your arms are straight.
Let it come back up until your forearms are about level.
benefits: Direct work for the triceps with steady cable resistance.
limitations: Needs a cable machine.
Trains a small muscle group only.

cues: Hang with your hands slightly wider than your shoulders, palms facing away.
Pull until your chin is over the bar.
Lower all the way under control.
benefits: Trains the back with your own body weight and only a bar.
limitations: Your body weight is the minimum load, which can be too much at first.

cues: Hands a little wider than your shoulders, body in a straight line.
Lower your chest towards the floor.
Push back up without letting your hips sag.
benefits: Needs no equipment.
Can be made easier with hands raised on a bench.
limitations: Harder to make heavier than a press with weights.

cues: Start with your arms straight on the bars.
Lower until your upper arms are about level with the floor, or as far as is comfortable.
Push back up.
benefits: Trains the chest and triceps with body weight.
limitations: Body weight is the minimum load.
The bottom position can be uncomfortable for some shoulders.

cues: Forearms under your shoulders, body in a straight line.
Squeeze your glutes and brace your stomach.
Breathe steadily and stop when your hips start to drop.
benefits: Trains the trunk to hold still, with no equipment.
limitations: Held for time, so it is harder to measure progress by weight.

cues: Elbow under your shoulder, body in a straight line.
Lift your hips and keep them up.
Do both sides.
benefits: Trains the side of the trunk with no equipment.
limitations: Each side is done separately.

cues: Hang from a bar without swinging.
Raise your legs, bending the knees to make it easier.
Lower slowly.
benefits: Trains the abdominals and hip flexors together.
limitations: Your grip has to hold your body weight.

cues: Hold a heavy dumbbell in each hand.
Stand tall and walk with short, steady steps.
Set the weights down under control.
benefits: Trains grip and trunk while walking.
limitations: Needs space to walk.

cues: Balls of your feet on the edge of the step.
Lower your heels for a stretch.
Rise as high as you can, then pause.
benefits: Direct work for the calves.
limitations: Needs a machine.

cues: Stand on one foot on the edge of a step, holding on for balance.
Lower your heel, then rise as high as you can.
Do both sides.
benefits: Needs only a step.
limitations: Each side is done separately.

cues: Pad on the front of your lower shins.
Straighten your knees.
Lower under control.
benefits: Direct work for the front of the thighs.
limitations: Needs a machine.

cues: Upper back on a bench, bar across your hips (a pad helps).
Drive your hips up until your body is level from shoulders to knees.
Lower under control.
benefits: Loads the glutes heavily without loading the spine from above.
limitations: Setting up the bar takes some time.

cues: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Push through your heels to lift your hips.
Pause at the top, then lower.
benefits: Needs no equipment.
limitations: Body weight alone is light for strong legs.

cues: Lie on your back with one foot flat and the other leg raised.
Push through the heel on the floor to lift your hips.
Keep your hips level; do both sides.
benefits: Harder than a two-leg bridge with no equipment.
limitations: Each side is done separately.

cues: Rear foot on a bench behind you.
Lower straight down until your front thigh is about level.
Push up through your front foot; do both sides.
benefits: Trains one leg at a time with light weights.
limitations: Balance takes practice.
Each side is done separately.

cues: Feet about shoulder-width apart.
Sit down and back, knees following your toes.
Stand up by pushing through your whole foot.
benefits: Needs no equipment.
limitations: Body weight alone is light for strong legs; more reps or a slower pace make it harder.

cues: Step back and lower your back knee towards the floor.
Keep most of your weight on the front foot.
Push back to standing; do both sides.
benefits: Needs no equipment and little space.
limitations: Each side is done separately.

cues: Dumbbells in front of your thighs, knees slightly bent.
Push your hips back with a flat back.
Stop when your hamstrings are stretched, then stand up.
benefits: The same movement as the barbell version with dumbbells.
limitations: The dumbbells you can hold limit the load.

cues: Slight bend in your elbows that stays the same.
Bring your hands together in front of your chest in a wide arc.
Open back out under control.
benefits: Chest work with steady cable resistance.
limitations: Needs a cable machine.

cues: Lie on a bench, dumbbells above your chest, elbows slightly bent.
Open your arms in a wide arc until you feel a stretch.
Bring them back together.
benefits: Chest work with dumbbells only.
limitations: Light weights only: the long arm position makes heavy loads hard to control.

cues: Feet on a bench, hands on the floor.
Body in a straight line.
Lower your chest, then push back up.
benefits: A harder push-up with no weights.
limitations: Harder to make heavier than a press with weights.

cues: Hang with your palms facing you, hands shoulder-width apart.
Pull until your chin is over the bar.
Lower all the way under control.
benefits: Trains the back and the biceps together with only a bar.
limitations: Your body weight is the minimum load.

exercises.equipment: A bar at waist height or a sturdy table
cues: Hang under a bar with your body straight, heels on the floor.
Pull your chest to the bar.
Lower until your arms are straight.
benefits: A rowing exercise with no weights; bending your knees makes it easier.
limitations: Needs a sturdy bar or table edge.

cues: Lie on a bench holding one dumbbell above your chest.
Lower it behind your head with slightly bent arms.
Bring it back over your chest.
benefits: Works the lats with one dumbbell.
limitations: Needs comfortable overhead shoulder movement.

cues: Rope at about face height.
Pull it towards your face, hands moving apart.
Return under control.
benefits: Direct work for the rear shoulders and upper back.
limitations: Needs a cable machine.

cues: Hinge forward with a flat back.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides with slightly bent elbows.
Lower slowly.
benefits: Direct work for the rear shoulders with light dumbbells.
limitations: Only light weights are practical.

cues: Hips high, body in an upside-down V.
Lower the top of your head towards the floor between your hands.
Push back up.
benefits: An overhead-style press with no equipment.
limitations: Harder to make heavier than a press with weights.

cues: Elbows by your sides.
Curl the bar up without swinging.
Lower until your arms are straight.
benefits: Both arms together with a load that is easy to increase.
limitations: Trains a small muscle group only.

cues: Palms facing each other.
Curl up without swinging.
Lower until your arms are straight.
benefits: Works the forearms more than a regular curl.
limitations: Trains a small muscle group only.

cues: Hold one dumbbell overhead with both hands.
Lower it behind your head by bending your elbows.
Straighten your arms.
benefits: Trains the triceps in a stretched position with one dumbbell.
limitations: Needs comfortable overhead shoulder movement.

cues: Hands on the edge of a bench behind you.
Lower by bending your elbows, as far as is comfortable.
Push back up.
benefits: Triceps work with only a bench.
limitations: The bottom position can be uncomfortable for some shoulders.

cues: Lie on your back, arms up, knees bent above your hips.
Press your lower back into the floor.
Lower the opposite arm and leg slowly, then switch.
benefits: Trains the trunk to stay still while the limbs move, with no equipment.
limitations: Easy to rush; it works only when done slowly.

terms.text: Three sets of 8 to 12 repetitions. A repetition (rep) is one complete movement; a set is a group of reps done without stopping. Rest, then do the next set.
Three sets of 40 seconds each, for exercises such as a plank where time is the target.
The lowest and highest number of reps you aim for in a set, such as 8–12. Choose a weight you can lift for at least the lowest number with good form.
The time between sets. The ACSM position stand suggests at least 2–3 minutes for heavier multi-joint lifts and 1–2 minutes for lighter accessory exercises.

How training is divided across the week. A full-body plan trains everything each session; a split gives different days different areas, such as upper and lower body. A 2024 meta-analysis found no significant difference in strength or muscle gains between split and full-body routines when weekly volume was the same.
Workouts follow a fixed order and you always do the next one, whichever day you train. The order carries on across weeks instead of restarting on Monday.
Each workout belongs to a weekday, such as Upper A on Monday. A missed workout stays on its day until you move or skip it.

A compound (multi-joint) exercise moves several joints and works several large muscles, such as a squat or a bench press. An accessory exercise usually moves one joint and works a smaller muscle, such as a curl. Compound lifts usually come first, while you are fresh.

Making training gradually harder so your body keeps adapting. The ACSM position stand suggests increasing the load by about 2–10% once you can do one or two reps more than your target in two sessions in a row.
How many sets a muscle group gets in a week. Comparisons between routines are fairest when weekly volume is the same.
